241.t: Reuben Roddy's saxophone style and hiring musicians
241.s: A saxophonist from Kansas City played a different style on the same beat; Thomas says he hired many men and gave them jobs.
241.q: Everybody played alike you know. That's why I tell you you've got to get an acquaintance for him. You see what I mean? You've got one style you've got to work the other style you see? So you've got to get acquainted with your style. See? How come you just went to see him and offered him a job with…

391.t: The alto player and the young tuba player
391.s: Keating and Allen discuss alto saxophonist Earl Batiste, who had played with R&B bands, Keating's dislike of saxophone, and the very young tuba player.
391.q: Uh, he seemed a very good musician. Uh, being a dyed in the wool, uh, Bunk Johnson and Lewis fan, uh, to be quite frank, no saxophone, uh, really moves me. Although, uh, having heard Manuel Paul, uh, play tenor, I found that quite interesting. Uh, but this, uh, lad was obviously a good musician.…

259.t: Joe Harris, alto saxophonist who worked with many bands
259.s: Vincent says Joe Harris played alto sax, not clarinet, worked with Earl Foster and many other bands, and played regular beer-garden jobs.
259.q: Say, how about Joe Harris? Joe Harris, he just used to play with a different fella. He's a good sucker for her. He was a good sucker for her. He was a good sucker for her. He wasn't talking to me. He wasn't out there yet. He wasn't good at that sucker for her. He was a good sucker for her.

251.t: Cottrell's tenor style and the band's saxophones
251.s: Louis Cottrell was the tenor soloist with his own tone; Hall doubled baritone.
251.q: Right. See, we had the clarinet wasn't a popular instrument in those days. It was the saxophones, the altos and the tenor. And of course, Hall doubled on the baritone. He got to sound like Duke's band. But on the feature, sometimes maybe Cottrell wanted to get away from his tunning, such as on the…

152.t: Session work through Cosmo and the move to baritone
152.s: Cosmo Matassa called the core of Bartholomew's band for sessions; he switched to baritone alongside Lee Allen on tenor.
152.q: Well, that came through Cosmo. That came through Cosmo. After we had done the recordings with Dave Bartholomew, there were calls that would come in that for Cosmo to get some musicians together. And the recording, the studio band was the nucleus of the Dave Bartholomew band. Earl Palmer, Frank…

191.t: Lake Charles musicians, fast alto players and Al Gallodoro
191.s: Allen asks about Nellie Lutcher and Paul Barnes; talk turns to fast-fingering alto players and Al Gallodoro's career.
191.q: Most certainly. He played all of those things. In fact, Galladero was really a great saxophonist and playing there's no question about it. And bassoon player. I didn't know he played bassoon.

830.t: Louis Warnick, alto saxophonist with Piron and Tio
830.s: They discuss Louis Warnick, who played alto sax with Piron and Lorenzo Tio and died in the 1950s, and Eddie Atkins.
830.q: And Louis Wani played for a long time. And I brought Eddie Atkins. He was in Chicago Eddie. He's been dead a long time. Eddie and Joe played for a long time. He's been dead. Did you have a Louis Wani played for a long time? Did you have a Louis Wani played for a long time? He played for a long…

118.s: Working the Playhouse with Harold Batiste, his tenor sax, and later California writing and a New Orleans studio.
118.q: Yeah. Yeah, I played the, I think with the, not the Playboy, I think with the, the Playhouse I used to work at on, I think it was St. Louis and Bourbon. And me and Bob Ostens, another good musician, Harold. What does Harold play? Harold played saxophone.

471.t: Earl Bostic's playing and rhythm and blues
471.s: Cobb describes Bostic as a top saxophonist who played rhythm and blues for a living.
471.ch: Bostic, Washington clubs and arriving in New York
471.q: Bostic was an A-1 saxophone, one of the better ones in the world. At one time in New York, when they used to have jam sessions, they had a thing where, a competition thing. The best guys on the stand could be on the stand. Like if you was up on the stand with Eddie Davis – Eddie “Lockjaw” Davis and…

225.s: Baker asks about Cecil Payne, known later on baritone; Johnson does not know why he focused on it.
225.q: Right. That’s interesting because, as you indicated, he became known as a baritone saxophone player and yet he was a very proficient soloist on alto saxophone. How he happened to himself perpetuate his image as a baritone saxophone [player] is interesting. I don’t know the answer to that. I guess…

1.t: Leonard Fields, the classical saxophone virtuoso who never got hired
1.s: Danny describes Leonard Fields's Rudy Wiedoft style and says the big bands overlooked him.
1.ch: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians
1.q: Because there was a man who was a helluva saxophone player, and he never got a chance. That was Fields(?). Fields(?) was a virtuoso. He played like this cat, Rudy Wiedoft.

377.t: The importance of tenor saxophones in the band
377.s: Basie says the two tenors were key figures, not specially arranged for, and that he likes tenor players.
377.ch: Building the band in New York
377.q: He was very important.. I mean, you he had two great tenor players there with Lester, in rehearsal. Very important and very instrumental in being key notes, key figures for the band. Tenors.

409.t: Charlie Holmes, Sam Taylor and Bob Dorsey
409.s: Cootie's saxophones included Charlie Holmes, Bob Dorsey and Sam The Man Taylor, who got few solos.
409.q: Yeah. A different sound or something. But Bob Dorsey used to play all the solos.

232.t: Leroy Cooper, the underrated baritone and lead saxophonist
232.s: Cooper later directed Ray Charles' band; Fields praises his willingness to play whatever dance music the crowd wanted.
232.q: Really, Leroy Cooper was one of my favorites among the sax that I did have, because he was just--why I lasted as long as I did, all along I would try to play for people. Now I liked when I had a musician if he was way out that was all right, but we're not going to do that all night, and I would try…

148.s: Handy found Boyd a horrible saxophonist who played every reed instrument for show.
148.ch: The Raeburn band: people and touring
148.q: I can't believe that anybody in this world that heard Boyd play saxophone could consider him a good saxophone player. In terms of the best to the worst, if he wasn't the worst, he was living the guy a hell of a run for the slot. He was a horrible saxophone player.
